title: The Science of Spoken Communication: What Research Tells Us

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Lim
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone. Today I want to look at what research actually tells us about spoken communication — specifically what makes communication more or less effective, and what we can do about it. I'll cover three areas: the role of non-verbal communication, the science of comprehension, and what we know about cross-cultural communication differences.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Lim
dialogue.text: Let's begin with non-verbal communication. A frequently cited figure — that 93% of communication is non-verbal — is a widespread misquotation of research by Albert Mehrabian from the 1960s. Mehrabian studied the communication of feelings and attitudes, not communication in general. His finding that people rely more on tone and facial expression than words, in ambiguous affective situations, has been extrapolated far beyond its original scope. The actual situation is more nuanced: non-verbal communication is crucially important, but its relative importance varies enormously by context.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Lim
dialogue.text: What we can say with confidence is this: in face-to-face communication, non-verbal cues — facial expression, eye contact, posture, gesture, and proxemics (the use of space) — are processed simultaneously with verbal content and often override it when the two conflict. If someone says "I'm fine" with a tense posture and averted eyes, listeners will typically disbelieve the verbal message. This is why written communication is more vulnerable to misinterpretation — the non-verbal channel is missing.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Lim
dialogue.text: Regarding comprehension: research on listening comprehension reveals that we process spoken language very differently from written language. In reading, we process text somewhat linearly, with the ability to re-read. In listening, we process in real time — information is transient. We rely heavily on prosodic cues — stress, rhythm, and intonation — to identify the information structure of utterances. We use our knowledge of context and discourse structure to predict what is likely to come next. And we rely on short-term memory, which is significantly more limited in listening than our intuition suggests.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Lim
dialogue.text: Interestingly, research shows that slightly slower speech — around 130 words per minute rather than the typical conversational rate of 150-200 — significantly improves comprehension for second-language listeners without sounding unnatural to native-speaker listeners. Pausing at appropriate junctures, rather than filling silence with hesitation markers, also improves comprehension. These are evidence-based recommendations for anyone who regularly speaks to mixed language audiences.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Lim
dialogue.text: On cross-cultural communication: the research here confirms many of the dimensions identified by Hofstede and Hall — differences in high versus low context communication, in attitudes to silence, in the management of disagreement. One consistently important finding is that the willingness to make explicit what is left implicit in one's own cultural setting — to over-communicate rather than assume shared background — significantly reduces miscommunication in intercultural contexts. This is sometimes called "accommodation to the interlocutor."

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Lim
dialogue.text: Let me close with what I think is the most practically important finding. Research on communication breakdowns consistently shows that the single most important skill for managing miscommunication is not linguistic accuracy — it is what researchers call "communication repair." The ability to recognise that communication has broken down, to seek clarification rather than proceeding on a false assumption, and to rephrase or reformulate when not understood — this skill predicts communicative success more reliably than any other single measure. In other words: it's not how well you speak, it's how well you deal with it when things go wrong.
